items.followUp: Differentiate between an ordered list and an unordered list in HTML.

rubric.why: Shows what a hyperlink does.
rubric.description: A hyperlink is a clickable text or image that opens another web page or resource.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a clickable link to another page or resource.

rubric.why: Shows what an anchor identifies or links to.
rubric.description: An anchor marks a location in a page, allowing a link to jump directly to that location.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the anchor as a marked destination or location within a page.

modelAnswer: A hyperlink is clickable text or an image that takes the user to another web page or resource.
An anchor marks a specific location in a page so a link can jump directly to it.

items.followUp: What is an ordered list in HTML? Give one example of its use.

rubric.why: Identifies the basic structure of a nested list.
rubric.description: A nested list is a list placed inside an item of another list.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one list is placed inside another list or list item.

rubric.why: Explains how the inner list relates to the outer list.
rubric.description: The inner list appears as a sublist under the relevant item of the main list.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the inner list as a sublist under an outer-list item.

modelAnswer: A nested list is a list placed inside an item of another list.
The inner list appears as a sublist under that item of the main list.

items.followUp: Explain how decomposition and abstraction help in solving a computer problem.

rubric.why: Recognises decomposition as a planning strategy.
rubric.description: Break the problem into smaller, manageable parts (decomposition).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing division of the problem into smaller parts.

rubric.why: Recognises pattern identification as a strategy.
rubric.description: Look for patterns or similarities among the parts or with previously solved problems.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining pattern recognition.

rubric.why: Recognises abstraction as a strategy.
rubric.description: Ignore irrelevant details and focus on the important information.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining abstraction or selecting relevant details.

rubric.why: Shows how the plan becomes a solution procedure.
rubric.description: Design an algorithm: an ordered set of steps to solve the problem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing an algorithm or an ordered solution procedure.

modelAnswer: Decomposition: Divide the problem into smaller, manageable parts.
Pattern recognition: Find similarities or repeated patterns in the parts or in previously solved problems.
Abstraction: Ignore irrelevant details and focus on the information needed to solve the problem.
Algorithm design: Write an ordered set of steps for solving the problem.

items.followUp: Define bus topology and draw a simple diagram of it.

rubric.why: Gives the meaning of network topology.
rubric.description: Network topology is the physical or logical arrangement of devices and connections in a network.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining topology as the arrangement or layout of a network.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining structure of ring topology.
rubric.description: In ring topology, each device is connected to two neighbouring devices, forming a closed loop.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the connected devices as a ring or closed loop.

rubric.why: Explains how data travels in a ring network.
rubric.description: Data travels from device to device around the ring, commonly in one direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing data transmission around the ring.

rubric.why: The diagram should show devices connected in a loop.
rubric.description: Draw and label a ring of connected computers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a diagram that clearly shows computers connected in a closed loop.

modelAnswer: Network topology is the physical or logical arrangement of devices and connections in a network.
In ring topology, each device is connected to two neighbouring devices, forming a closed loop.
Data travels from one device to the next around the ring, commonly in one direction.
Diagram:
[Computer 1] ─── [Computer 2]
[Computer 4] ─── [Computer 3]

items.followUp: Describe two ways software piracy can occur.

rubric.why: Identifies copying or sharing software without permission.
rubric.description: Softlifting is making or using unauthorized copies of software, such as installing one licensed copy on several computers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for softlifting or unauthorized copying/sharing.

rubric.why: Identifies piracy by sellers who install unlicensed software.
rubric.description: Hard-disk loading is when a seller installs illegal copies of software on computers before selling them.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for hard-disk loading and its meaning.

rubric.why: Identifies the sale of fake copies as piracy.
rubric.description: Counterfeiting is making and selling software copies that imitate the genuine product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for counterfeiting and its meaning.

rubric.why: Identifies unauthorized distribution or downloading through the internet.
rubric.description: Online piracy is illegally downloading or distributing software over the internet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for online piracy and its meaning.

modelAnswer: Softlifting: Making or using unauthorized copies of software, for example, installing one licensed copy on several computers.
Hard-disk loading: A seller installs illegal software on a computer before selling it.
Counterfeiting: Making and selling fake copies that imitate genuine software.
Online piracy: Illegally downloading or distributing software over the internet.

items.followUp: What questions should be asked when using the five Ws to understand a problem?

rubric.why: Lists the five questions used to understand a problem.
rubric.description: The five Ws are Who, What, Where, When and Why.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for correctly listing all five; award 1 mark for three or four.

modelAnswer: We use the five Ws to gather information and understand a problem clearly before planning its solution.
The five Ws are Who, What, Where, When and Why.

items.followUp: Name one strategy for planning a solution and explain how it helps.

rubric.why: Identifies reuse of an existing solution as the time-saving strategy.
rubric.description: Reusing an existing solution, or part of one, saves time when it fits the problem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying reuse or an existing solution.

rubric.why: Explains why reuse is useful.
rubric.description: The existing solution can be adapted or modified instead of starting from scratch, saving time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the time saved by adapting rather than creating a solution from the beginning.

modelAnswer: Reusing an existing solution saves time.
If it is suitable, we can adapt or modify it instead of creating a new solution from the beginning.

items.followUp: What is boundary test data? Give one example.

rubric.why: Includes data that lies within the accepted range.
rubric.description: Normal (valid) test data is acceptable data within the permitted range.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming normal or valid data.

rubric.why: Includes data that should be rejected.
rubric.description: Abnormal (invalid or erroneous) test data is outside the permitted range or has an incorrect format.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming abnormal, invalid or erroneous data.

modelAnswer: The types of test data are:
Normal (valid) data.
Abnormal (invalid or erroneous) data.
Boundary data, which tests values at the limits of the permitted range.
